doc.title: Clay Jenkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 18, 2016

title: Whom he calls for gigs and why pianists should lay out
summary: He wouldn't call unpleasant players and likes pianists who comp little; Harold Danko's story of the doctor praises laying out.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom

blocks.x: Very interesting. Like most musicians, I’m guessing you have a list, under all instruments you have your list. I’m going to say this question from a backwards standpoint. What gets people less likely to be called by you? What makes a musician sort of move down your list as far as filling a gig?

Well if they’re not a nice person. If they’re not a nice person I usually don’t — we’ve got to get along. I mean I know some really great players I wouldn’t call because they don’t strike me as nice men or women. That would be the first thing. I don’t like it when piano players comp too much. I like it when they don’t comp very much. Harold Danko is a fantastic comper and he doesn’t comp very much at all. I mean sometimes when he does you don’t notice it because he’s just very economical.
I’m glad to hear you say that because I think sometimes musicians in small groups don’t realize that, especially for piano or guitar, by not playing they’re adding a texture.

That’s a great point, yeah. Harold Danko told me a great thing. He said he was playing in New York and he did three nights at The Kitano. And he said there was a very well- dressed gentleman there all three nights and at the end of the third night the guy walked up to him and said, “I’m not a musician, I’m a doctor.” And Harold said, “well it’s nice to meet you.” And he said, “I’ve got to tell you,” he said, “but if I was a piano player I’d like to know how to lay out just like you.” I thought that was great. You’re right. By not playing they’re adding a texture. You’re so right. And another thing I tell my guys, you know there’s something about a trio — there’s something very special about a trio that’s the art of the trio. But there’s something special about a trio. If a horn player’s playing with a group and everybody’s playing then he doesn’t get a trio. So I like it when piano players don’t play because then I get a trio. I like having a trio. Because there’s very special nuance and magic that happens with a trio. So when a piano player doesn’t play or the guitar player doesn’t play then I’ve got the — or if the drummer doesn’t play. But
piano players tend not to do that. You know? So I really encourage them to get out of there.
Do you actually suggest that to them sometimes?
Well if no one’s ever told them — I think it’s so obvious that people don’t actually think of it. Like it’s more like it’s wrong to not play. Like gee I’m not playing, this isn’t right.
Well I’ve had students like get mad at me for telling them to lay out. Even if the guitar player’s comping, some piano players want to comp too. So yeah that’s a great point.
